blocks.text: But Ol. Celsius in Hierobot. vol. 2, p. 82, rightly points out that there is no lack of examples of others who, in the want of a long siege, turned to food things that human nature otherwise abhors. "Wretched mortals," he says, "shudder at perishing of hunger so long as anything remains, however foul and abominable, by which they may put off the fatal moment. Hence histories everywhere record that many have yielded to necessity and in sieges have used even the excrement of animals as food and drink." Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. book 3, ch. 6, writes of the final siege of the Jews: "Necessity set everything before their teeth in place of food, and they brought themselves to eat things that would not have been fit even for the most unclean brute beasts. — For some, even the stalks of old hay served as food. Some gathered refuse." In Josephus, Jewish War book 6, last chapter, near the end, we read: προσελθῶν τινὰς εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀνάγκης, ὥστε τὰς ἀμάρας ἐρευνῶντας καὶ παλαιὸν ὄνθον βοῶν, προσφέρεσθαι τὰ ἐκ τούτων σκύβαλα, καὶ τὸ μηδὲ ὄψει φορητὸν πάλαι τότε γενέσθαι τροφήν [proselthōn tinas eis tosouton anankēs, hōste tas amaras ereunōntas kai palaion onthon boōn, prospheresthai ta ek toutōn skybala, kai to mēde opsei phorēton palai tote genesthai trophēn]. "Some were driven to such necessity that they searched the sewers and took the old dung of oxen as nourishment, and the collected filth, which before had not been bearable even to look at, became food." And in Brusonius, Memorabilia book 2, ch. 41: "The Cretans, when Metellus besieged them, quenched their thirst with the urine of beasts of burden for lack of wine and water." Cipriano de Valera, in the marginal notes to the Spanish version at 2 Reg. VI, 25: En el Epitome de las chronicas de Inglaterra se dize, que año de 1316 (que fue el año 10 del rey Eduardo 2.) huvo tanta hambre en Inglaterra, que los pobres comian sus criaturas, perros, ratas, y estiercol de palomas. That is: in the Epitome of the Chronicles of England it is said that in the year 1316 (which was the 10th year of the reign of Edward II) there was so great a famine in England that people ate their own infants, dogs, mice, and dove's dung. To these examples adduced by Celsius I add a very similar one from Abdollatif, Compendium of the Memorable Things of Egypt book 2, ch. 2, p. 119 of the octavo edition. In the great famine that raged in Egypt in the year 1200 AD [II, 574] 1200, اكلوا الميتات والجيف والكلاب والبعر والاروات [akalū al-maytāt wa-al-jiyaf wa-al-kilāb wa-al-baʿr wa-al-arwāt] they fed on the dead, on stinking carcasses, on camel dung and on dung. The annals of the Orientals are full of examples of this kind.
Iliad. 9, 214. Πάσσε δ' ἁλὸς θείοιο [passe d' halos theioio].
Forsskål described the varieties of Salsola Kali in Flora Aegypt. Arab. p. 54 ff. Compare with him Rauwolf, Travels p. 37, Augsburg edition, 1583.

Suaeda monoica in Forsskål, p. 70, who, after describing it carefully, adds: "This is the plant from which the Arabs of Yemen extract alkali salt, in a dilute solution of which clothes are washed before they are treated with soap."
Rauwolf, p. 37, confirms that Salsola Kali is used for making glass.
